Route on the map

How the packets travelled

Each row is one probe. It leaves your computer with a TTL that equals the row's number. The circle on every router it crosses shows the TTL left after that router subtracted 1. Where the TTL reaches 0 the router drops the probe and answers with an ICMP error, so each reply tells you who sits at that distance.

The located hops add up to about 14,446 km. Light in fibre covers roughly 200 km per millisecond, so a round trip over that distance cannot be faster than about 144 ms. The last answer took 214 ms, 1.5× that floor. Real routes are longer than the straight line between cities, and every router adds queueing and processing time.

What happened at each hop

TTL 1 · 192.168.1.1

Default gateway (your router)private (RFC 1918)RTT min/avg/max 1.1 ms / 1.2 ms / 1.3 ms
  1. You send a UDP datagram with IP TTL=1 to 203.0.113.10.
  2. No router sits before this one, so the probe arrives with TTL=1.
  3. The router subtracts 1, gets 0 and discards the packet (RFC 1812).
  4. It sends ICMP type 11, code 0 (time exceeded in transit) from 192.168.1.1 to you. The error quotes the dropped packet's IP header plus 8 bytes of its payload.
  5. Traceroute matches it to the probe using the UDP source and destination ports quoted inside the ICMP error. RTT = 1.2 ms on average.
  • Hop 1 is the next device on your local link. Your computer sends probes to its MAC address after an ARP lookup.

TTL 11 · 203.0.113.10

Destination hostdocumentation rangeAshburn, United StatesRTT min/avg/max 213.9 ms / 214.4 ms / 214.8 ms
  1. You send a UDP datagram with IP TTL=11 to 203.0.113.10.
  2. The 10 routers before this one each subtract 1 from TTL, so it arrives here with TTL of 1 or more.
  3. The destination accepts the packet. Nothing listens on the high UDP port, so the destination's IP stack answers with an ICMP error. That error is how traceroute knows it arrived.
  4. It replies with ICMP type 3, code 3 (destination unreachable: port unreachable). Traceroute matches it to the probe using the UDP source and destination ports quoted inside the ICMP error.
  5. RTT = time the reply arrived minus time the probe left: 214.4 ms on average.

What each device and program does

1 · vis_route.py on your computer

ApplicationValidates the target (IPv4 or hostname, never an option string), resolves a hostname with a DNS A lookup, then starts the system traceroute as a child process with an argument list, so no shell is involved.
tracerouteFor TTL 1, 2, 3 … it sends 3 probes per TTL. It sets the TTL on the socket (setsockopt IP_TTL), calls sendto() and reads ICMP errors from a raw ICMP socket. It prints one line per hop.
TransportUDP header: random source port, destination port 33434 and up (one per probe).
NetworkKernel builds the IPv4 header: TTL=k, protocol 17, destination 203.0.113.10. The routing table picks the default route.
LinkARP finds the gateway's MAC address (cached). The NIC sends an Ethernet or Wi-Fi frame addressed to the gateway.

2 · Your home router

LinkReceives the frame and strips the Ethernet header.
NetworkChecks the TTL. If it is 1 the router stops here and sends ICMP time exceeded; otherwise it subtracts 1 and updates the header checksum.
NATRewrites your private source address and port to its own public (or ISP-NAT) address and stores a connection-tracking entry. That entry lets an ICMP error coming back be translated to your private address.
ForwardingLooks up the next hop (usually the ISP) and re-frames the packet for the uplink (PPPoE, Ethernet, GPON).

3 · Each transit router

IngressLine card receives the packet and parses the IP header.
LookupLongest-prefix match in the forwarding table picks the egress port. With equal-cost routes it hashes the addresses and ports, so probes of one traceroute can split across paths.
TTLTTL−1, checksum update, forward. At TTL 0 the packet is dropped and handed to the control-plane CPU.
ICMPThe CPU builds ICMP type 11 code 0, sourced from one of its own addresses, and sends it toward you. Routers rate-limit this, so these hops show higher or patchier RTT than real traffic sees. MPLS networks can hide hops entirely.
ReturnThe error is routed independently. The way back can be a different path than the way out.

4 · Destination host

Link / IPFrame accepted, destination address 203.0.113.10 matches the host, TTL is not an issue.
TransportNothing listens on the high UDP port, so the destination's IP stack answers with an ICMP error. That error is how traceroute knows it arrived.
ReplyICMP type 3, code 3 (destination unreachable: port unreachable). After this reply traceroute stops.
If silentA firewall or a host that ignores this probe type gives a run of * * * at the end. Another --method often gets through.

5 · vis_route.py after the trace

ParseReads each output line, collecting responder addresses and RTTs. Handles Linux, macOS and Windows layouts, lost probes and several responders per TTL.
ClassifyPrivate, CGNAT and documentation addresses are never sent anywhere.
GeolocateFor each public hop: local cache first, then one HTTPS request to the geolocation service (DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, GET /json/<ip>, JSON reply, 5 s timeout). --offline skips the network.
DrawBasemap draws the map. Great-circle arcs join consecutive located hops.
WritePNG map, JSON data and this HTML report go to the output folder.

Highlighted cells are the fields that make traceroute work. Italic cells are typical values that differ per machine. Sizes follow the default probe (60 bytes).

Reading the numbers: a hop's RTT includes the time its router needs to generate the ICMP error, so it is not a clean measure of the link. Locations come from a geolocation database and can be off by hundreds of kilometres, especially for routers. Addresses shown are the ones routers put in their replies, which are not always the interface the probe came in on.
